Geographic focus:
    Europe (Switzerland, Basel)

Temporal focus:
    T1. Historical report [YES] — references post-GFC bank behavior
    T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES] — Swiss parliament upcoming discussions on UBS capital requirements
    T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [YES] — structural capital adequacy framing for next downturn cycle

Synopsis:
    SNB Vice Chairman Antoine Martin argued that higher capital buffers are not a competitive handicap for banks, citing post-GFC evidence where well-capitalized institutions gained market share. His comments are timed ahead of Swiss legislative debate on stricter capital rules for UBS, and carry an implicit regulatory nudge: Swiss banks should be positioned to absorb stress and capture share from weaker foreign rivals in the next downturn.

Q01. Is the content relevant to US economy, US yields, US interest rates and US stock market pricing?
Relevance: IMPLICIT — The commentary is Swiss-centric but carries indirect relevance: tighter global bank capital standards affect cross-border lending, credit conditions, and large US financial sector names. A more capital-constrained UBS also impacts global liquidity dynamics.

Q02. Is the content confirming already known information or reporting very new/uncertain risks?
Risk score: 15 — The general direction of post-Credit Suisse regulatory tightening for UBS is well-telegraphed. Martin's comments reinforce an already-anticipated regulatory trajectory; no surprise pivot here.

Q03. Is the content explicitly about bullish impact on the US stock markets?
Explicit: NO
Impact score: 5 — Marginally bullish only insofar as a more resilient global banking system reduces systemic tail risk, but this is indirect and weak.

Q04. Is the content explicitly about bearish impact on the US stock markets?
Explicit: NO
Impact score: 10 — Slightly bearish at the margin for global bank equities and credit availability if capital requirements tighten further and constrain balance sheet deployment, but the direct US market impact is minimal.
